a: I have put a king over you
t: A farewell speech at a turning point
p: Samuel's speech closes the age of the judges and opens the age of the kings.
b: Samuel hands over leadership but not his voice. The speech reviews God's record (12:6–11), Israel's record (12:12), and sets terms for the future (12:14–15, 12:20–25), the pattern of a covenant renewal. Martin Noth noticed that the Deuteronomistic History marks its turning points with speeches like this: Joshua's farewell (Joshua 23), this one, Solomon's prayer (1 Kings 8) and the sermon on Samaria's fall (2 Kings 17). Critical scholars (the C lens) hear the editor's voice here. Traditional readers (H) see Samuel's own words, preserved by the prophetic writers of 1 Chronicles 29:29. Either way, Samuel does not retire: he keeps the role of prophet and intercessor (12:23).

a: before his anointed one
t: "His anointed": the first king called messiah
p: The word behind "Messiah" here means the reigning king, Saul.
b: The Hebrew is meshicho, "his anointed one," from mashach, "to smear with oil." Hannah had already sung of the LORD's "anointed" (2:10), and now the title has a living holder: Saul, anointed by Samuel (10:1). In 1 Samuel the phrase almost always means the reigning king, and David will refuse to touch Saul for that reason (24:6; 26:9). Greek translates it christos. So when later Jews and Christians spoke of "the Messiah" or "the Christ," they were using a royal title that began with kings like Saul and David.

a: Whose ox did I take? Whose donkey did I take?
t: What kings take, Samuel never took
p: Samuel answers his own warning that a king "will take" sons, daughters, fields and flocks.
b: In chapter 8 Samuel warned that a king would take: sons, daughters, fields, vineyards, servants and donkeys (8:11–17). Now he asks whether he ever took anything, and the people agree that he did not (12:4). The contrast is deliberate. Moses made the same defense when Korah's band accused him: "I have not taken one donkey from them" (Numbers 16:15). The law forbade judges to take bribes (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19). Samuel's own sons had broken that rule (8:3), which is part of why the people asked for a king.

a: I will take you to court before the LORD
p: Samuel speaks like a prosecutor: the people are in court, and the LORD's record is the evidence.
b: The verb shafat in the reflexive form means "go to law with, argue a case against." Samuel calls Israel into court and lists "the LORD's just deeds" (Hebrew tsidqot), the same word the Song of Deborah uses for God's victories (Judges 5:11). The prophets later use the same courtroom shape, the covenant lawsuit, to put Israel on trial (Micah 6:1–5; Isaiah 1:2–20; Jeremiah 2:4–13). The Plain English "all the ways the LORD has done right by you" tries to keep both senses of tsidqot: acts that were just, and acts that saved.
orig: וְאִשָּׁפְטָה (ve'ishshafetah), "and let me go to law"; צִדְקוֹת (tsidqot), "just deeds"

a: he sold them into the power of Sisera
t: The book of Judges in one breath
p: Samuel's summary follows the cycle of Judges: forget God, be sold, cry out, be rescued.
b: Each step uses the vocabulary of Judges: Israel "forgot" the LORD (Judges 3:7), he "sold them" (Judges 4:2; Judges 10:7), they "cried out" and confessed (Judges 10:10), and he sent rescuers (Judges 2:16). Sisera is the general of Hazor defeated by Deborah and Barak (Judges 4–5), the Philistines oppress Israel in Judges 10:7 and 13:1, and the king of Moab is Eglon (Judges 3:12–30). The list is not in time order, which suggests Samuel is picking well-known examples rather than giving a timeline.

a: Jerubbaal
p: Jerubbaal is Gideon, who once refused to be king (Judges 8:23).
b: Gideon was given the name Jerubbaal when he tore down Baal's altar (Judges 6:32). Samuel may name him first for a reason: when the Israelites offered Gideon a crown, he answered, "The LORD will rule over you" (Judges 8:23). That is exactly Samuel's point in the next verse. The list ends with Samuel himself, which is unusual but not boastful: he includes himself in the line of rescuers God sent. On the names Barak and Samuel in this verse, see the textual notes.

a: And all the while the LORD your God was your king.
t: Why did Israel ask for a king?
p: Chapter 8 blames Samuel's corrupt sons; here Samuel blames fear of Nahash. How do the two fit?
b: In chapter 8 the elders ask for a king because Samuel is old and his sons take bribes (8:1–5). Here Samuel says they asked when Nahash the Ammonite attacked (ch. 11). Critical scholars (C) see two sources with different explanations, and an anti-monarchy strand that treats the request as rejecting God (8:7; 10:19; 12:17). Traditional readers (H) note that both motives can be true, since the Ammonite threat was building for some time (4QSam-a at 10:27 says Nahash had been oppressing the tribes east of the Jordan). Either way, Samuel's charge is the same one Gideon made: Israel already had a king.

a: the king you asked for
p: The name Saul (Sha'ul) means "asked for," and the story keeps playing on it.
b: "Asked for" is she'eltem, from sha'al, "to ask." Saul's name, Sha'ul, is the passive form of the same verb: "the one asked for." The narrator uses the pun again and again: the people "asked for" a king (8:10; 12:17; 12:19). Oddly, the same pun is attached to Samuel's birth: Hannah "asked" him from the LORD and "lends" him back (1:20; 1:28). Some scholars (McCarter, for example) think the birth story was first told of Saul. Others think the narrator links the two men on purpose: one was asked from God, the other asked for against God's wishes.

a: then you and the king who rules you will be followers of the LORD your God
p: The Hebrew "if" clause never gets a clear "then." Translations fill the gap differently.
b: The verse lists conditions (fear, serve, listen, do not rebel) and then says, word for word, "and you will be, both you and the king who reigns over you, after the LORD your God." It can be read as the "then" ("then you will be following the LORD"), as one more condition with the result left unsaid ("... then all will be well," as some versions add), or as a promise of protection ("you will be in the LORD's train"). The Plain English takes the first, since "to be after" someone in Hebrew often means "to follow" him (2 Samuel 2:10). The threat in 12:15 has a clear result, which makes the missing result here stand out.
orig: וִהְיִתֶם גַּם־אַתֶּם וְגַם־הַמֶּלֶךְ ... אַחַר יְהוָה (vihyitem gam-attem ... achar YHWH)

a: Isn't this the wheat harvest?
p: Wheat is cut in May and June, the heart of the dry season, when rain almost never falls in Israel.
b: Israel's rains come from about October to April. By the wheat harvest in late spring, the sky is usually clear for months, and rain could ruin grain lying in the fields. Proverbs uses it as a picture of something out of place: like snow in summer and rain at harvest, honor does not fit a fool (Proverbs 26:1). A thunderstorm on command is both a sign and a threat. It also answers the Canaanite belief that Baal, the storm god, sent the rain: the LORD rules the sky. The Hebrew for thunder is qolot, "voices," the same word Exodus uses at Sinai (Exodus 19:16).

a: hollow things
t: Tohu: the word for chaos and idols
p: Samuel uses the word that describes the earth before creation, "shapeless."
b: Tohu is the word in Genesis 1:2, where the earth is "shapeless and empty" (Genesis 1:2). It means emptiness, a void, something with no substance. Isaiah uses it of idols and the people who make them: "all of them are tohu" (Isaiah 44:9; Isaiah 41:29). Samuel does not name the idols, but the word points to the Baals and Ashtoreths of 12:10. They cannot "help" or "rescue," the two things Israel needed most. The Greek translation adds the word "gods" to make the idols explicit, but the Hebrew lets the emptiness speak for itself.

a: His great name is at stake.
t: "For the sake of his great name"
p: The Hebrew says the LORD acts "because of his great name," that is, for the sake of his reputation.
b: Word for word: "For the LORD will not abandon his people, for the sake of his great name." A god who let his people be destroyed would be thought weak by the nations, so his "name," his reputation and honor, is bound up with Israel's survival. Moses argued the same way when he prayed for Israel after the golden calf (Exodus 32:12; Numbers 14:13–16), and Ezekiel says God acts "for my holy name" (Ezekiel 36:22). The second half gives the deeper reason: God "took it upon himself" (ho'il, "was willing, undertook") to make Israel his people. He started this, and he will finish it.

a: I will never sin against the LORD by giving up praying for you
t: Failing to pray as a sin
p: Samuel treats prayerlessness for his people as a sin against God. The Talmud builds a rule on this verse.
b: Samuel loses his office but keeps two tasks: praying and teaching. Jeremiah 15:1 and Psalm 99:6 remember him with Moses as the great intercessors. The Talmud draws a rule from this verse: anyone who can ask mercy for his neighbor and does not is called a sinner (Berakhot 12b). Christians have read it alongside Paul's "we have not stopped praying for you" (Colossians 1:9) and the call to pray for all people and for kings (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Samuel's prayer here is notable because the people he prays for have just rejected his leadership.

a: you and your king alike will be swept away
p: The last word of Samuel's speech looks ahead to the fall of the kingdoms and the exile.
b: "Swept away" (tissafu) is the word Abraham used when he asked whether God would sweep away the righteous with the wicked at Sodom (Genesis 18:23). Readers of the finished history knew how it ended: kings and people were carried off, Israel by Assyria (2 Kings 17) and Judah by Babylon (2 Kings 25). The speech is therefore read as a key to the whole story of the kings that follows. The next chapters test it at once: within a short time Saul himself fails to listen to the LORD's voice (13:13; 15:19).

a: He ruled over Israel [...] two years.
p: The Bible never gives a clear number. Estimates range from two to forty years; most historians guess about twenty.
b: The Hebrew verse is damaged (see the textual note). Paul's sermon in Acts says Saul reigned forty years (Acts 13:21), perhaps a round number from tradition. Josephus also reaches forty in one passage (Antiquities 6.378), though his manuscripts disagree. The story itself points to a reign of some length: Jonathan is already a commander here (13:2), and Saul's son Ish-bosheth was forty when his father died (2 Samuel 2:10). Many historians date Saul to roughly 1030–1010 BC. The plain fact is that the number was lost early, and no ancient source preserves it with certainty.

a: a thousand stayed with Jonathan
p: Saul's son steps into the story already a commander, without any introduction.
b: Jonathan's name, Yehonatan, means "the LORD has given." He leads a third of Saul's standing army, so he is an adult and a proven fighter. That tells us time has passed since Saul was a "young man" looking for donkeys (9:2). The first thing Jonathan does in the story is strike the Philistines (13:3), and the first thing he does in the next chapter is strike them again. In 1 Samuel he is the son who acts while his father waits, and the friend who gives David what should have been his own (18:4; 23:17).

a: the Philistine post in Geba
p: The Hebrew netsiv can mean a garrison, an official stationed in a town, or a pillar set up as a sign of rule.
b: Netsiv comes from a root meaning "to stand, set up." It can mean a body of troops stationed somewhere (a garrison or post), a governor or prefect (1 Kings 4:19 uses it for Solomon's district officers), or a standing pillar or monument (Genesis 19:26 uses the same word for Lot's wife, a "pillar" of salt). The Philistines had one at Gibeath-elohim (10:5). If it was an official or a pillar, Jonathan's act was a deliberate act of rebellion against Philistine rule. Geba and Gibeah, two Benjaminite towns a few miles apart, are easily confused in the Hebrew and in the versions.

a: east of Beth-aven
p: Michmash sits on a ridge north of a deep gorge; Geba lies on the ridge to the south.
b: Michmash is the modern village of Mukhmas, about seven miles north of Jerusalem. Between it and Geba runs a steep ravine, the Wadi Suweinit, with cliffs on both sides; that is the "pass of Michmash" (13:23) where Jonathan will climb (14:4–5). Isaiah traces an invader's route through the same places (Isaiah 10:28–29). Beth-aven ("house of wickedness" or "house of strength") was a town near Ai (Joshua 7:2). Hosea later uses the name as a mocking nickname for Bethel (Hosea 4:15), but here it seems to be a separate place.

a: Hebrews went across the Jordan
p: The Hebrew plays on the name: the 'Ivrim (Hebrews) 'averu (crossed over).
b: In Samuel the word "Hebrews" is used mostly by Philistines or in contrast to them (4:6; 13:19; 14:11; 29:3), sometimes as a slightly scornful outsider's term. Here the narrator makes a pun: the 'Ivrim 'averu, the Hebrews "crossed" the Jordan to escape. Many scholars connect the word with the 'apiru (Habiru) of the Amarna letters and other texts of the 1300s BC: landless people, raiders and hired soldiers on the edges of society. Others think the similarity is only partial, and that "Hebrew" is simply an ethnic name, as in Genesis 14:13. See 14:21 for Hebrews who fought for the Philistines.

a: until the time Samuel had fixed
t: The seven days and Samuel's lateness
p: Saul is waiting because of an order Samuel gave him at his anointing (10:8). Readers disagree on how fair the test was.
b: When Samuel anointed Saul he said, "Wait seven days until I come to you" at Gilgal (10:8). Saul waits until the seventh day; Samuel arrives as soon as he finishes. Some readers think Saul did all he could and was trapped (Gunn's "fate of King Saul"). Others point out that Saul did not wait until the end of the seventh day, and that the order was a test of whether the king would put the prophet's word above military pressure (V. Philips Long). Critical scholars note that 10:8 seems to expect this scene right away, so chapters 11–12 may have been placed between them later. Traditional readers think the order covered the first call to war, whenever it came.

a: Then he offered up the burnt offering.
p: Kings did offer sacrifices in Israel. So why is this wrong?
b: David and Solomon both offered sacrifices without blame (2 Samuel 6:17–18; 1 Kings 3:4; 1 Kings 8:62–64), so it is not simply that a king did a priest's job, though later Jewish readers often saw it that way (compare Uzziah, 2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Samuel's own charge is that Saul "did not obey" a specific command of the LORD given through the prophet (13:13). Others see the sacrifice as a war ritual meant to force God's hand, a use of religion as magic. Literary readers notice that Saul has a reason for everything (13:11–12), a pattern that returns in chapter 15.

a: You have acted like a fool
p: "Fool" in Hebrew means more than unwise: it means acting against God and good sense.
b: The verb is sakhal. Saul will use the same word of himself near the end: "I have played the fool" (26:21), and David uses it when he confesses his census (2 Samuel 24:10). In Hebrew wisdom writing the fool is not stupid but willful, someone who does not take God into account (Psalm 14:1). The opposite word, sakal, "to act wisely, succeed," is used again and again of David (18:5; 18:14; 18:30). The two kings are being compared by their wisdom.

a: a man to suit his own heart
p: The famous phrase may describe David's character, or simply mean a man of God's own choosing.
b: The Hebrew is ish kilvavo, "a man according to his heart." Traditionally it is read as a statement about David's devotion: he would share God's heart and do his will, as Paul's sermon puts it (Acts 13:22). Some scholars (McCarter, among others) note that the same phrase in 14:7 means "as you wish": the armor-bearer tells Jonathan to do "according to your heart." On that reading, God has chosen a man by his own choice, unlike Saul, whom the people chose. Both senses fit the story: God picks David (16:1–13), and David is also praised for loyalty to God (1 Kings 11:4; 1 Kings 15:3).

a: ruler
p: Samuel does not say "king" here but nagid, a title for the ruler God has picked.
b: Nagid means "leader, one placed in front." In Samuel and Kings it is the word God uses when he designates a ruler: Saul (9:16; 10:1), David (here; 25:30; 2 Samuel 5:2; 2 Samuel 7:8), and later kings (1 Kings 14:7; 1 Kings 16:2). Scholars such as Tryggve Mettinger argue that it means "king-designate," the one chosen before he takes the throne. The word lets the narrator stress that the ruler is God's appointee and answers to him, whatever the people call him.

a: The destroyers
p: The Hebrew calls the Philistine raiding force "the destroyer," the same word used for the angel of death in Egypt.
b: Hammashchit is a participle: "the one who destroys." It is used of the destroyer who struck Egypt's firstborn (Exodus 12:23) and of the angel who struck Jerusalem in David's time (2 Samuel 24:16). Here it names the raiding columns that went out to plunder the countryside, which is why many versions say "raiders." The Plain English keeps the harsher word because the narrator repeats it (14:15).

a: There was no smith to be found in the whole land of Israel.
p: The text says the Philistines kept Israel from making weapons. Archaeology gives a more mixed picture.
b: For much of the 1900s scholars took this verse as evidence that the Philistines held a secret of ironworking, learned from the Hittites, and kept it from Israel. Later study changed that picture. Iron tools spread slowly across the whole region in the 1100s–900s BC, and Philistine sites do not show more iron than others at first. The verse does not mention iron; it says there was no charash, "smith" or metalworker, in Israel. Most historians now read it as a policy of political control: the Philistines kept the hill people dependent and disarmed, as later empires did (2 Kings 24:14).

a: a pim
p: For centuries no one knew what a pim was. Archaeologists found small weights marked pym.
b: The KJV guessed "a file." Then, from the early 1900s on, excavators in Judah found small stone weights inscribed pym, weighing about 7.5 to 8 grams, roughly two-thirds of a shekel. The verse is a price list: a pim to sharpen a plow blade or hoe, a third of a shekel for smaller tools. It is also evidence that this passage reflects real life in the monarchy: once the pim weight went out of use, the word was forgotten. The Plain English keeps "pim" and gives the meaning in the gloss.

a: under the pomegranate tree in Migron
p: While his son climbs a cliff, Saul sits under a tree. Literary readers see a deliberate contrast.
b: The chapter opens with two pictures side by side: Jonathan setting out with one companion (14:1), and Saul sitting at the edge of town with six hundred men and a priest (14:2–3). Deborah also "used to sit" under a tree to judge (Judges 4:5), but Saul's sitting is not judging; he is waiting, as he waited at Gilgal. Readers of the L lens note that through the chapter Saul reacts to events (14:16–19), makes rash vows (14:24) and asks God too late (14:37), while Jonathan acts in faith (14:6). Migron is also named in Isaiah 10:28, apparently north of Michmash, which suggests there were two places of the name or that the text has been disturbed.

a: Ahijah was there too, carrying the ephod
t: A priest from the doomed house of Eli
p: Ahijah's family tree links him to Eli, whose house God had condemned (2:27–36).
b: The narrator takes care to trace Ahijah back through Ahitub and Phinehas to Eli, "the LORD's priest at Shiloh." Readers of chapters 2–4 know that Eli's sons died, Ichabod was born the day the ark was lost, and a man of God foretold the end of Eli's line (2:30–36). Saul's religious support comes from that house. The ephod he carries is not the linen apron of 2:18 but the priest's oracle garment with its pouch for the Urim and Thummim (Exodus 28:6–30). Many think Ahijah is the same man as Ahimelech son of Ahitub, the priest of Nob whom Saul later kills (22:9–20).

a: One was called Bozez, the other Seneh.
p: Bozez may mean "shining" or "slippery"; Seneh means "thorny," the word for the burning bush.
b: The two crags stand on either side of the Wadi Suweinit, the gorge between Geba and Michmash. Seneh is the word for the "bush" Moses saw burning (Exodus 3:2); Bozez is less certain, perhaps "gleaming" from the white chalk rock. The north crag faces Michmash and the south faces Geba (14:5). In his memoir, the British officer Vivian Gilbert tells how in February 1918 a brigade major read this chapter, found the path Jonathan climbed, and led troops up it to surprise the Turkish force at Michmash. The story rests on Gilbert's account alone and is not confirmed in the official histories. Whatever its details, the geography of the chapter fits the land closely.

a: these uncircumcised men
p: The Philistines were the one neighboring people who did not circumcise. The word becomes an insult.
b: Egyptians, Edomites, Ammonites and Moabites practiced circumcision in some form (Jeremiah 9:25–26), but the Philistines, who came from the Aegean, did not. So "uncircumcised" becomes Israel's shorthand for the Philistines (31:4; Judges 14:3; Judges 15:18), and David will use it of Goliath (17:26; 17:36). For Jonathan it is more than a sneer: these men stand outside the covenant whose sign was circumcision (Genesis 17:10–14), so the LORD is not on their side.

a: He can save with many or with few.
t: Victory does not depend on numbers
p: Jonathan states a theme that runs from Gideon's three hundred to the Maccabees.
b: God cut Gideon's army to three hundred so Israel could not say, "My own hand rescued me" (Judges 7:2). Asa prays, "For you there is no difference in helping, whether the side is great or has no strength" (2 Chronicles 14:11), and Zechariah hears, "Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit" (Zechariah 4:6). Judas Maccabeus told his small army almost the same thing as Jonathan: "To Heaven it makes no difference whether it saves by many or by few" (1 Maccabees 3:18). "Heaven" is that book's name for God. David will make the same point before Goliath (17:47).

a: That is the sign for us.
p: Jonathan lets the enemy's words decide his move. Was that faith or fortune-telling?
b: Jonathan sets up a test: if the Philistines say "come up," that is the sign. Abraham's servant did something like it at the well (Genesis 24:12–14), and Gideon tested God with the fleece (Judges 6:36–40). The law forbade looking for omens (Leviticus 19:26). Rav in the Talmud takes the signs of Abraham's servant and of Jonathan as the very model of the omen-taking the law forbids (Hullin 95b). Later commentators (Tosafot, Ran) explain why these two were allowed: Jonathan was going to fight anyway, or the sign had a reasonable basis. Most Christian readers have taken Jonathan's sign as an act of faith that leaves the outcome to God, not a superstition. The difference, they say, is that Jonathan was already committed to fight; the sign only told him when.

a: inside a space about half a furrow long
p: The Hebrew is unclear. The Greek translators read something completely different.
b: Word for word the Hebrew says "as in half a furrow, a yoke of field." A "yoke" (tsemed) was probably the land a team of oxen could plow in a day, so the phrase seems to mean the twenty men fell within a very small area, perhaps half an acre. The point is how fast and close the fighting was. The Septuagint reads "with darts and with stones and with pebbles of the field," which suggests its Hebrew text had different words here, or that the translators guessed. Modern translations follow the Hebrew, with notes.
orig: כְּבַחֲצִי מַעֲנָה צֶמֶד שָׂדֶה (kevachatsi ma'anah tsemed sadeh)

a: It was a trembling from God.
t: A panic sent by God, or a very great panic?
p: Hebrew sometimes adds "of God" to mean "very great." Here both senses fit.
b: The phrase is cherdat elohim. In Hebrew, "of God" can make a superlative: "a mighty prince" is literally "a prince of God" (Genesis 23:6), and the KJV here has "a very great trembling." But the chapter clearly means God is at work: the ground shakes, and the panic turns the enemy against itself (14:20). This is the classic sign of the LORD fighting for Israel, as at the Sea (Exodus 14:24), Gibeon (Joshua 10:10) and Gideon's night attack (Judges 7:22). The Plain English keeps "from God" so readers can see both.

a: "Pull your hand back," Saul told the priest.
p: The priest's hand was probably in the ephod's pouch, about to draw the lot. Saul does not wait for the answer.
b: Saul had asked for God's guidance (14:18). The priest reached for the sacred lot, the Urim and Thummim kept in the ephod (Exodus 28:30). But the noise from the Philistine camp grew, and Saul told him to stop. He went into battle without God's answer. Readers note the pattern: at Gilgal Saul would not wait for Samuel (13:8–12), here he will not wait for the oracle, and later, when he does ask, God will not answer him (14:37; 28:6). The same impatience runs through all three scenes.

a: There were Hebrews who had sided with the Philistines
p: The text separates "Hebrews" who fought for the Philistines from "the Israelites with Saul."
b: This verse treats "Hebrews" and "Israelites" as different groups. Some Hebrews had gone up with the Philistine army; now they switch sides. For many scholars this fits the idea that 'ivri was related to the 'apiru of older texts, people without a fixed place who hired themselves out as soldiers. Others take the Hebrews here to be Israelites who had been forced into Philistine service. Later David himself will serve a Philistine king with his own band of men, and the Philistine commanders will ask, "What are these Hebrews?" (29:3).

a: A curse on anyone who eats food before evening
p: Saul binds the whole army to fast in the middle of a battle. It weakens them and nearly costs Jonathan his life.
b: Fasting before battle was a way of seeking God (Judges 20:26), and an oath could set an army apart for holy war. But Saul's oath is about himself: "until I take revenge on my enemies." It leaves the troops too faint to finish the job (14:28–31) and leads them to sin by eating meat with the blood (14:32). Many readers compare Jephthah, whose rash vow cost his daughter's life (Judges 11:30–40). This time the people step in and save the victim (14:45). The Greek text says plainly that Saul "made a great blunder" that day (see the textual note).

a: there was honey lying out on the open field
p: The Hebrew ya'ar usually means "forest," but can also mean "honeycomb." Both may be meant.
b: The same word appears in 14:26: the people came "into the forest" (ya'ar), and in 14:27 Jonathan dipped his stick into "the comb of honey" (ya'rat haddevash). In Song of Songs 5:1, ya'ar means "honeycomb." Wild honey from bees nesting in rocks and trees was a real food (Deuteronomy 32:13; Judges 14:8; Matthew 3:4). The scene is meant to tempt: food lying free on the ground for a starving army that has sworn not to touch it.
r: 14:26–27; Song of Songs 5:1; Deuteronomy 32:13; Judges 14:8; Matthew 3:4

a: his eyes lit up
p: In Hebrew, eyes that "brighten" mean strength and life coming back.
b: The scribes' reading (the Qere) is "his eyes brightened"; the written text (the Ketiv) reads "his eyes saw." Either way, the sense is that Jonathan revived. Dim eyes are a sign of weakness, hunger and approaching death (Psalm 6:7; Psalm 38:10), and bright eyes a sign of renewed life (Psalm 13:3; Ezra 9:8). Jonathan's point in 14:29 is practical: a little food would have given the whole army strength.

a: My father has stirred up trouble for the land.
p: Jonathan uses the word 'akhar, "to bring trouble," the word linked to Achan.
b: When Achan took what was under the ban, Joshua asked him, "Why have you brought trouble on us?" (Joshua 7:25), and the place was named the Valley of Achor, "trouble." Jephthah used the same word to his daughter (Judges 11:35), and Ahab and Elijah would trade it (1 Kings 18:17–18). Jonathan applies it to his father, the one who made the oath. The irony is sharp: the lot will soon point at Jonathan as the guilty one, as it pointed at Achan, but the real troubler is the king.

a: the people ate them, blood and all
p: The law forbade eating blood. Saul's hungry troops slaughtered animals on the ground and ate at once.
b: "Do not eat anything with the blood" (Leviticus 19:26). The blood was the life, and it belonged to God (Genesis 9:4; Leviticus 17:10–14; Deuteronomy 12:23–24). Proper slaughter let the blood drain out, usually on an altar or poured on the ground. Here the starving men killed the animals "on the ground" and ate on the spot. Some scholars read the Hebrew 'al-haddam as "over the blood," a pagan rite of eating near the poured-out blood (Ezekiel 33:25). Saul's fix is practical: a large stone becomes a slaughtering table so the blood can drain away (14:33–34).

a: this was where he started building altars to the LORD
p: The Hebrew can mean this was Saul's first altar, or that he began to build it and did not finish.
b: The Hebrew says, "it he began to build as an altar to the LORD." Most read it as "this was the first altar he built." Some Jewish commentators read "he began" more literally: Saul started the altar but, in his hurry to chase the Philistines (14:36), did not finish it. Either way the story notes Saul's new piety after a day of rash oaths and blunders. Literary readers set it beside the altar-building of the patriarchs (Genesis 12:7; Genesis 35:7) and Samuel (7:17), and ask whether Saul's religion is sincere or a substitute for obedience (15:22).
orig: אֹתוֹ הֵחֵל לִבְנוֹת מִזְבֵּחַ (oto hechel livnot mizbeach)

a: No answer came from him that day.
p: For the first time God does not answer Saul. It will happen again at the end of his life.
b: Saul asks the right question at last, but there is no answer. Silence from the oracle meant something was wrong between the people and God, so Saul looks for the sin (14:38). In chapter 28 the silence will be total: the LORD answers Saul neither by dreams nor by Urim nor by prophets (28:6), and Saul turns to a medium. Readers differ on whether the silence here is a punishment for Saul's oath, for the people eating blood, or a sign of the LORD's withdrawal from Saul that will be stated openly in 16:14.

a: let Urim come out
t: How the Urim and Thummim worked
p: The longer Greek text shows the sacred lot as a yes-or-no device with two possible answers.
b: Nothing in the Bible describes the Urim and Thummim. This verse, in the longer form preserved by the Septuagint (see the textual note), is the clearest window: each possible answer is matched to one of the two objects. Saul divides the people into two groups, then the remaining two people, until one is left (14:42). That fits a two-sided lot, perhaps stones or sticks drawn from the pouch of the ephod. In Joshua 7:14–18 a similar step-by-step process found Achan. Proverbs 16:33 states the belief behind it: the lot is cast into the lap, but its decision comes from the LORD.

a: Here I am, ready to die.
p: Jonathan's words can be read as calm acceptance or as an indignant question.
b: The Hebrew is hineni amut, "here I am, I will die." It can be a brave statement: Jonathan accepts the verdict, the way a soldier would. Or, with a change of tone, it can be a question full of protest: "for a taste of honey, must I die?" Many modern readers hear the protest, since Jonathan has already called the oath a mistake (14:29–30). The text gives no stage directions, and readers have heard Jonathan both ways.

a: So the people ransomed Jonathan
p: The verb padah means "to buy back." It may mean the people paid something in Jonathan's place.
b: Padah is used for redeeming a firstborn son or animal by a payment or a substitute (Exodus 13:13; Exodus 34:20; Numbers 18:15–16). So the people may have offered an animal or money in Jonathan's place, which would satisfy the oath. Or the word may be used loosely: they simply rescued him. Either way, the army overrules the king, and Saul gives in. Readers often compare Jephthah's daughter, whom no one ransomed (Judges 11:34–40), and note that the oath Saul swore to protect the army almost killed the man who won the battle.

a: Ishvi
t: Saul's sons and the name Baal
p: Ishvi is probably the son elsewhere called Eshbaal or Ish-bosheth.
b: The lists of Saul's sons do not quite match. Here: Jonathan, Ishvi, Malchishua. At his death: Jonathan, Abinadab, Malchishua (31:2). In Chronicles: Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab and Eshbaal (1 Chronicles 8:33). The son who reigned after Saul is called Ish-bosheth, "man of shame," in 2 Samuel (2:8), and Eshbaal, "man of Baal" or "the Lord exists," in Chronicles. Many think scribes replaced "Baal" with "shame" (boshet) when the word came to mean only the Canaanite god. "Ishvi" may be another softened form, perhaps "man of the LORD" (Ish-yo).

a: Abner son of Ner, Saul's uncle
p: Abner was Saul's cousin (or perhaps uncle), the commander who later made and unmade kings.
b: The Hebrew can mean that Ner was Saul's uncle, making Abner his cousin, which 14:51 supports: Kish and Ner were both sons of Abiel. But 1 Chronicles 8:33 and 9:36–39 make Ner the father of Kish, which would make Abner Saul's uncle. Abner will be the strongman who keeps Saul's house alive after Gilboa, then defects to David and is murdered by Joab (2 Samuel 2–3). He appears in David's story in 17:55 and 26:5–16.

a: Any time Saul spotted a powerful man or a man of courage, he drew him into his own ranks.
p: Saul does exactly what Samuel said a king would do: take Israel's sons for his army.
b: "He will take your sons and put them in his chariots and among his horsemen" was Samuel's warning (8:11). The chapter ends with Saul building a standing army from the best men he can find. The next thing he takes into his service is a young man from Bethlehem (16:21–22). The note prepares for David's arrival at court, and it shows that Saul's kingship, for all its failures, does what Israel asked a king to do: "fight our battles" (8:20).

a: hear the sound of the LORD's words
t: Qol: the key word of chapter 15
p: "Sound" and "voice" are one Hebrew word, qol. The chapter turns on whose voice Saul hears.
b: Samuel opens with "listen to the qol of the LORD's words." The word returns as the "sound" of sheep in Samuel's ears (15:14), the question "Why did you not listen to the LORD's voice?" (15:19), Saul's claim "I did listen to the LORD's voice" (15:20), Samuel's verdict that listening is better than sacrifice (15:22), and Saul's confession that he "listened to their qol," the people's (15:24). English cannot use one word for all of these, so the Plain English uses "sound" and "voice." The Hebrew shama' beqol, "listen to the voice," is the normal way to say "obey."

a: I have kept count of what Amalek did to Israel
p: The command goes back to Amalek's attack on Israel after the Exodus.
b: Amalek attacked Israel at Rephidim (Exodus 17:8–16). Moses wrote that the LORD would wipe out the memory of Amalek, and Deuteronomy commands: "Remember what Amalek did to you on the road when you came out of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 25:17), adding that Amalek cut down the weak stragglers at the rear (Deuteronomy 25:18). The verb here, paqad, means "to take note of, to visit, to settle accounts." Amalekites still raided Israel in the time of the judges (Judges 6:3; Judges 10:12), so the old enemy was a living threat. The rabbis read the passage on the Sabbath before Purim as the prophetic reading (haftarah) for Shabbat Zakhor, "the Sabbath of Remembering."

a: put all they have under the ban
p: Few passages trouble modern readers more. Jews and Christians have answered it in different ways.
b: Cherem, "the ban," gave everything to God by destroying it (Deuteronomy 20:16–18; Joshua 6:17–21). Readers answer the moral problem in several ways. Traditional readers (H) see a one-time judgment on a people with a long record of attacks (Genesis 15:16). Evangelical scholars such as Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan, following Lawson Younger's study of ancient conquest reports and Nicholas Wolterstorff, argue the language is stock war rhetoric meaning "defeat decisively," since Amalekites survive (27:8; 30:1). Others, such as Eric Seibert, hold that such texts reflect Israel's view of God, which later revelation corrects. Critical scholars (C) see a later ideology, not a record of events. The Talmud gives Saul himself the moral protest: if a whole heifer is broken for one unsolved killing (Deuteronomy 21:1–9), how much more for all these lives? If the adults sinned, what did the children and animals do? A heavenly voice answers, "Do not be righteous too much" (Ecclesiastes 7:16; Yoma 22b). Maimonides rules that peace must be offered first even to Amalek (Laws of Kings 6:1–4). Later Jewish authorities held that the ancient nations can no longer be identified, so the command cannot be carried out.

a: two hundred thousand on foot
p: The figures are huge for the time. Some read "thousand" as a military unit.
b: Two hundred thousand soldiers would be an enormous army for the hill country of Israel around 1000 BC, when whole towns had a few hundred people. The Hebrew 'elef means "thousand," but it also means a clan or a military unit (10:19; Judges 6:15), so some scholars read "two hundred units." Others take the numbers as deliberate exaggeration, common in ancient war records, or as accurate. The Greek text gives even larger figures. On the problem in general, see the census topic.

a: the Kenites
t: The Kenites and an old kindness
p: The Kenites were kin to Moses' father-in-law and lived alongside Amalek in the south.
b: Moses' father-in-law is called a Kenite (Judges 1:16; Judges 4:11), and Moses had asked his family to travel with Israel as guides (Numbers 10:29–32). Kenites settled in the Negev among the people of Judah and near Amalek (Judges 1:16). Jael, who killed Sisera, was the wife of a Kenite (Judges 4:17). Saul honors an old hesed, "loyal love," by warning them away. Even in a war of total destruction, the text insists on telling friend from foe. David will later share his plunder with the Kenite towns (30:29).

a: from Havilah on the way to Shur
p: The same boundary marks where Ishmael's descendants lived (Genesis 25:18).
b: Shur is the desert on the eastern border of Egypt (Genesis 16:7). Havilah is uncertain, probably somewhere in northwestern Arabia. The phrase is almost word for word the description of Ishmael's people: they lived "from Havilah to Shur, which faces Egypt" (Genesis 25:18). It describes the whole desert range of the nomads south of Judah rather than a single march. Saul struck Amalek across its home territory, but the Amalekites who raid Ziklag in chapter 30 show that he did not wipe them all out.

a: the second-year animals
p: The Hebrew mishnim is odd here. It may mean second-born animals or be a slip for "fat ones."
b: Mishnim means "second" or "doubles." Jewish commentators explained it as animals born second, which were thought to be better, or animals two years old. Many modern scholars change one letter and read mashmannim, "fatlings, fat ones" (as in Nehemiah 8:10), which suits "the pick of the sheep and cattle" and "all that was good." Some versions follow the Targum and Syriac in a similar direction. The meaning is clear in any case: Saul and the people kept the best and destroyed the worst.

a: Saul and the people took pity on Agag
p: Saul "took pity" on what God told him not to pity. Readers ask what the pity was really about.
b: The verb chamal, "to pity, to spare," is the same word as the command "Have no pity on them" (15:3). The narrator shows Saul sparing the king and the best animals, and destroying only what was "cheap and worthless." That looks less like mercy than like keeping the valuable spoil, which is what Samuel will charge (15:19). The Talmud, though, imagines Saul arguing from mercy (Yoma 22b; see the note on 15:3). Saul's later excuse, that the animals were for sacrifice (15:15; 15:21), may be honest or may be cover. Achan also took the best of what was banned (Joshua 7:21). Sparing a captured king was common in the ancient world, as a trophy or for ransom.

a: I regret making Saul king.
p: The verb nicham is used of God "regretting" here and in 15:35, and of God not regretting in 15:29.
b: Nicham covers regret, grief, a change of mind, and comfort. God "regrets" or "is sorry" that he made humankind before the Flood (Genesis 6:6). Balaam says God is not a human being "that he should change his mind" (Numbers 23:19), using the same verb. Chapter 15 puts both ideas within a few verses: the LORD regrets making Saul king (15:11; 15:35), yet Israel's Enduring One "does not regret" (15:29). The Plain English uses "regret" every time so readers can see the tension the Hebrew puts there. On how readers resolve it, see the note at 15:29 and the topic page.

a: Samuel was hot with anger
p: Hebrew says "it burned to Samuel." That usually means anger. At whom, the text does not say.
b: Vayyichar leShmu'el, "it burned for Samuel," is the normal idiom for anger (18:8; Genesis 4:5). The KJV softened it to "it grieved Samuel," and some versions say "distressed." If the anger is real, its target is open: Saul, who failed; the LORD, who had made him king and now rejected him; or himself, who had anointed him. Samuel's next act is to cry out to the LORD all night, an act of intercession like his prayers in 7:9 and 12:18, and like Moses' after the golden calf.

a: he is putting up a monument to himself
p: The Hebrew calls the monument a yad, "hand," the word behind Israel's Holocaust memorial, Yad Vashem.
b: A yad, literally "hand," is a standing stone or pillar that marks a place or a name. Absalom set one up for himself because he had no son to keep his name alive (2 Samuel 18:18). Isaiah promises faithful eunuchs "a hand and a name" (yad vashem) better than sons and daughters (Isaiah 56:5), the source of the name of Israel's Holocaust memorial. Saul's monument celebrates his victory while he is in the very act of disobeying. This Carmel is a town in the hills of Judah south of Hebron (25:2), not the mountain by the sea.

a: the LORD your God
p: Three times Saul speaks to Samuel of "the LORD your God." Readers ask what that says about Saul.
b: Saul says the animals were spared for "the LORD your God" (15:15), taken to sacrifice to "the LORD your God" (15:21), and asks to worship "the LORD your God" (15:30). It may only be polite speech to a prophet, as people often spoke to Elijah or Elisha (1 Kings 17:12; 2 Kings 19:4). But many readers hear distance: Saul treats the LORD as Samuel's God, not his own. Samuel, by contrast, speaks of "the LORD" who anointed "you" (15:17).

a: You may think yourself small
p: Samuel reminds Saul how he began: shy, from the smallest tribe, hiding among the baggage.
b: When Samuel first spoke to him, Saul protested that he came from the smallest tribe and the least family in Benjamin (9:21), and on the day of his choosing he hid among the baggage (10:22). Samuel turns that humility back on him: the man who thought himself small was made head of the tribes. Now he fears "the people" (15:24) more than the God who raised him. The theme of the small one chosen goes on in the next chapter: David is "the smallest" of Jesse's sons (16:11).

a: Does the LORD take as much pleasure in burnt offerings and sacrifices
t: Obedience and sacrifice in the prophets
p: Samuel's saying is the first of many prophetic words that put obedience above ritual.
b: Samuel does not reject sacrifice; he ranks it. The same theme returns in the prophets and Psalms: Hosea 6:6 ("I want loyal love, not sacrifice"), Amos 5:21–24, Micah 6:6–8, Isaiah 1:11–17, Jeremiah 7:21–23, Psalm 40:6–8, Psalm 51:16–17 and Proverbs 21:3. Jesus twice quotes Hosea's form of it (Matthew 9:13; Matthew 12:7), and a scribe agrees that love of God and neighbor is worth more than all burnt offerings (Mark 12:33). Jewish readers have used the verse to teach that offerings without obedience are worthless, and, after the temple fell, that prayer and good deeds could take the place of sacrifice. Christians have read it with Hebrews 10:5–10, where the obedience of Christ fulfills the sacrifices.
r: Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21–24; Micah 6:6–8; Isaiah 1:11–17; Jeremiah 7:21–23; Psalm 51:16–17; Proverbs 21:3; Matthew 9:13; Matthew 12:7; Mark 12:33; Hebrews 10:5–10

a: the fat of rams
p: The fat was the part of an animal offering that belonged to God.
b: In Israel's sacrifices, the fat around the organs was burned on the altar: "All the fat belongs to the LORD" (Leviticus 3:16). It was the richest part of the animal, so "the fat of rams" means the best offering a person could bring. Samuel's line says that even the best offering is worth less than attention to God's voice. The Hebrew lehaqshiv, "to pay attention, to prick up the ears," is a word the prophets use for listening to God (Isaiah 48:18; Jeremiah 6:10).

a: Rebellion is the sin of fortune-telling
p: The Hebrew is compressed and hard. Its point: disobeying God is as bad as the pagan practices Saul despised.
b: Word for word: "For the sin of divination is rebellion, and wickedness and teraphim is pushing." Qesem is divination, forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10 ("anyone who practices divination"). Teraphim are household gods (see the topic). Haftsar comes from a verb "to press, urge": stubborn insistence on one's own way. The sense: defying God is as serious as consulting other powers. The irony is that Saul banned mediums from the land (28:3) but will end by consulting one (28:7–19). The KJV's "witchcraft" is too narrow; qesem covers all fortune-telling.

a: "I have sinned," Saul said to Samuel.
p: Saul says "I have sinned" twice and is not restored. David says it once and is forgiven. Why?
b: Saul confesses (15:24; 15:30), but his reasons stay the same: he feared the people, and he wants honor before the elders (15:30). David, faced with a far worse sin, says only "I have sinned against the LORD" and hears that the LORD has taken away his sin, though there are still consequences (2 Samuel 12:13–14). Many readers find the difference in the heart of each confession, as in Psalm 51. Others, especially in the tragic reading (Gunn, Exum), find Saul treated more harshly than David for lesser failings, and take the story as a hard look at a God whose choice of David is not fully explained. Both readings start from the same verses.

a: carry away my sin
p: The usual Hebrew word for forgiving sin is nasa', "to lift, carry."
b: Saul asks Samuel, literally, to "lift my sin." The same verb describes God "forgiving guilt, rebellion and sin" (Exodus 34:7), Joseph's brothers asking him to forgive (Genesis 50:17), and the goat that "carries" Israel's sins into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:22). Saul asks the prophet to carry it, as if Samuel could release him. Samuel refuses (15:26).

a: he caught at the corner of his robe, and it ripped
p: Hebrew does not say whose hand tore whose robe. The tear becomes a picture of the torn kingdom.
b: The Hebrew says only "he took hold of the corner of his robe." Most readers, and the Greek translation, take it that Saul grabbed Samuel's robe, a gesture of pleading known from other ancient texts (Ronald Brauner). Some interpreters have suggested that Samuel tore Saul's robe. Either way Samuel makes it a sign: the LORD has torn the kingdom from Saul (15:28). The image returns when David cuts the corner of Saul's robe in the cave (24:4–5), when Ahijah tears his cloak into twelve pieces for Jeroboam (1 Kings 11:29–31), and at Endor, where Samuel appears wearing a robe (28:14).

a: Israel's Enduring One does not lie and does not regret
p: Six verses after God regrets making Saul king, Samuel says God does not regret. How do readers fit them together?
b: Several answers are given. (1) Different senses: in 15:11 God grieves over what happened; in 15:29 he will not take back the verdict on Saul. Many Jewish commentators, such as Radak, take this line. (2) Human language: God speaks of himself in human terms so people can understand, but does not change (Maimonides; Calvin, Institutes 1.17.12–14). (3) Real responsiveness: God does react to human choices, but he is not fickle like a human (15:29 says "he is not a human being"), a view held by many modern theologians, and pressed further by open theists. (4) Critical readers see two layers in the text. The title netsach Yisrael, "Israel's Enduring One," is unique; the Greek reads "Israel will be split in two" (see the textual note).

a: Agag came to him in chains
p: The Hebrew word here is rare. It may mean "cheerfully," "in chains" or "trembling."
b: Ma'adannot is pointed in the Hebrew as if from 'adan, "delight": "cheerfully, delicately" (so the KJV, "delicately"). But the same letters can come from 'anad, "to bind" (Job 38:31 uses the word for the "chains" of the Pleiades), giving "in fetters." The Greek has "trembling." Each choice changes the scene: a confident king who thinks the danger is over, a captive dragged in chains, or a frightened man. The Plain English takes "in chains," which fits a prisoner brought before the prophet, and reads Agag's words that follow (see the textual note) as hope rather than swagger.

a: And Samuel hacked Agag to pieces before the LORD at Gilgal.
t: Samuel's act and the shadow of Haman
p: Samuel carries out the ban himself. Jewish tradition tied Agag's line to Haman.
b: "Before the LORD" marks the execution as a religious act, completing the ban Saul left undone. Samuel's poem uses the rule of measure for measure: as Agag's sword made mothers childless, his mother will be. Haman, the enemy of the Jews in Esther, is called "the Agagite" (Esther 3:1), and Mordecai is a Benjaminite descended from Kish, like Saul (Esther 2:5). Jewish tradition reads Esther as the final settling of this account; a legend says Agag fathered a child in the night before his death, and Haman came from that line. Modern readers often find the scene hard to read; others see the prophet doing what the king refused to do.

a: Samuel never saw Saul again until the day he died
p: Samuel and Saul meet again in 19:24. "See" probably means a formal visit.
b: In 19:18–24 Saul comes to Ramah and lies before Samuel, prophesying. Many explain that "not see again" means Samuel never again went to visit Saul or met him as his prophet; the meeting at Ramah is Saul's doing, not Samuel's. Critical scholars think the two passages come from different sources. Either way the end of the relationship is sad: Samuel "mourned" for Saul, and the LORD has to tell him to stop (16:1). In death, Samuel will meet Saul once more, at Endor (28:11–19).

a: I have seen a king for myself among his sons
t: "I have seen": the chapter about seeing
p: God says he has "seen" a king, meaning chosen or provided one. Seeing is the theme of the whole chapter.
b: Ra'iti means "I have seen," and here "I have picked out, provided." Abraham told Isaac, "God will see to the lamb" (Genesis 22:8), and named the mountain "The LORD Will See" (Genesis 22:14). The verb runs through the chapter: Samuel "saw" Eliab (16:6); the LORD tells him not to look at appearances, for God does not see as people see (16:7); a servant has "seen" a son of Jesse (16:18). Saul was the king the people asked for; this one is the king God saw "for myself."

a: Jesse the Bethlehemite
p: David's father is the grandson of Ruth and Boaz. Bethlehem becomes the town of the Messiah.
b: The book of Ruth ends: "Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David" (Ruth 4:22). So Jesse's grandmother was Ruth the Moabite. Bethlehem, "house of bread," was a small town in Judah, about six miles south of Jerusalem. Isaiah speaks of a shoot from "the stump of Jesse" (Isaiah 11:1), and Micah of a ruler who will come from Bethlehem Ephrathah (Micah 5:2), a promise the Gospels see fulfilled in Jesus (Matthew 2:1–6; Luke 2:4). "Jesse" is named here rather than David himself: God's choice comes before the reader even learns the boy's name.
r: Ruth 4:17–22; Isaiah 11:1; Isaiah 11:10; Micah 5:2; Matthew 2:1–6; Luke 2:4

a: Take a heifer from the herd along with you.
t: Did God tell Samuel to deceive?
p: God gives Samuel a true but partial reason for his trip. Jewish and Christian readers have debated what this permits.
b: Samuel really does offer a sacrifice (16:5), so what he says is true; he simply does not say everything. The Talmud uses this verse to teach that one may change the truth for the sake of peace, and one rabbi says it is even a duty (Yevamot 65b). Augustine, who held that every lie is a sin, made a distinction often cited here: hiding the truth is not the same as telling a lie. Most Christian readers have followed him, seeing a lawful concealment to protect life rather than a lie. Modern readers also note how dangerous Samuel's mission was: anointing a rival king was treason.

a: Have you come in peace?
p: A visit from a prophet could mean judgment. The elders want to know if trouble has come.
b: Samuel was a judge as well as a prophet; he went on a circuit to judge Israel (7:15–17). An unexpected visit from such a man might mean an accusation, a sacrifice for some guilt, or news of war. The last time he acted publicly, he cut a captive king to pieces (15:33). The question "Is it peace?" (shalom) is a standard nervous greeting (2 Kings 9:17–22; 1 Kings 2:13). The widow of Zarephath also asked a man of God whether he had come to bring her sin to mind (1 Kings 17:18).

a: Make yourselves holy
p: To "make yourselves holy" meant washing and keeping away from anything that made a person unclean.
b: The verb qadash in this form means to set oneself apart for God. Before Sinai, the people had to wash their clothes and keep apart from sex for two days (Exodus 19:10–15). Before a sacrifice and its shared meal, a person had to be ritually clean (Leviticus 7:20–21). Samuel himself sees to it for Jesse and his sons. The detail matters later: David is not there for the rites, because he is out with the sheep (16:11).

a: A human sees what is before the eyes, but the LORD sees the heart.
p: One of the best-known verses in Samuel. Its point is aimed at Samuel himself.
b: Samuel had once presented Saul because he was taller than everyone (10:23–24), and now he is ready to anoint the tall Eliab. God's answer applies to prophets as well as people. The Hebrew is clipped: "for not what the human sees," with no verb for God; the Greek fills it in as "for God does not see as a human sees." The verse became a key text for the belief that God knows the heart (1 Kings 8:39; Jeremiah 17:10; Psalm 139:1–4; Luke 16:15; Acts 1:24). Literary readers note the irony that David turns out to be handsome too (16:12): looks are not the reason for the choice, but they are not ruled out.

a: seven of his sons
t: How many sons did Jesse have?
p: Here and in 17:12 Jesse has eight sons. Chronicles lists seven, with David the seventh.
b: 1 Samuel counts eight sons: seven pass before Samuel, and David makes eight (17:12). 1 Chronicles 2:13–15 lists seven by name, with David seventh. Some readers think one son died young and was left out of the later list; others think Chronicles shaped the list so David would be the seventh, the number of completeness. The three oldest are named the same in both: Eliab, Abinadab and Shammah (Shimea).

a: The smallest one is left
p: Again and again in the Bible, God passes over the oldest son and picks a younger one.
b: Haqqatan means both "the youngest" and "the smallest." God chose Abel's offering over Cain's, Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Joseph and then Judah over Reuben, Ephraim over Manasseh, and Moses, the youngest of three. Gideon was the least in his father's house (Judges 6:15). David's case fits the pattern and also the theme of this chapter: the one no one thought to call, off with the sheep, is the one God has seen. Psalm 78:70–71 remembers it: God took David from the sheepfolds to shepherd his people.
r: 15:17; Genesis 4:4–5; Genesis 21:12; Genesis 25:23; Genesis 48:14–20; Judges 6:15; Psalm 78:70–71

a: He had a reddish glow
p: Admoni means reddish: perhaps red hair, perhaps a ruddy complexion. It is also the word used of Esau.
b: Admoni describes Esau at birth: "The first one out was red" (Genesis 25:25). Whether David had red hair or a healthy ruddy skin is not clear; Song of Songs 5:10 praises a lover as "glowing and ruddy" with the related word adom. A Jewish midrash says Samuel was afraid when he saw David was ruddy, thinking he would be a shedder of blood like Esau, but God answered that this one would kill only by lawful judgment (Genesis Rabbah 63:8).

a: anointed him there among his brothers
p: Only now does the narrator give the boy's name. The anointing was done in front of his family, not in public.
b: This is the first time the name David appears in 1 Samuel (in Christian order he is already named in Ruth 4:17 and Ruth 4:22). Its meaning is uncertain; most connect it with dod, "beloved" or "uncle," and some with a title for a leader. Samuel anoints him in front of his brothers, but no one says what the anointing means; Eliab's scorn in 17:28 suggests the family did not grasp it. David will be anointed twice more, publicly, by Judah (2 Samuel 2:4) and by all Israel (2 Samuel 5:3). The horn of oil is a contrast with the small "flask" used for Saul (10:1).

a: the LORD's Spirit swept down on David
p: The Spirit "swept down" on judges for a moment. On David it stays "from that day on."
b: The verb tsalach, "to rush, sweep down," is used of the Spirit coming on Samson (Judges 14:6; Judges 15:14) and on Saul (10:6; 10:10; 11:6). For them it came at a moment of need. Here the narrator adds "from that day on." The next verse says the LORD's Spirit had turned away from Saul (16:14): the gift passes from one king to the other. David's prayer "your holy spirit, do not take it from me" (Psalm 51:11) is often read against this background. Christians see a pattern fulfilled when the Spirit comes down and remains on Jesus (John 1:32–33).

a: an evil spirit from the LORD kept terrifying him
t: An evil spirit from the LORD?
p: The text says the spirit that tormented Saul came from God. Readers have explained it in very different ways.
b: The Hebrew ra'ah means "evil" or "harmful," and some versions say "harmful spirit" or "spirit of distress." The Targum says "an evil spirit from before the LORD." Readers have taken the spirit as (1) a demon God allowed to afflict Saul, the view of Josephus (Antiquities 6.166), many church fathers and some rabbis; (2) a messenger of judgment sent by God, like the spirit God sent between Abimelech and Shechem (Judges 9:23) or the lying spirit of 1 Kings 22:19–23; (3) an illness of mind. That last view is not only modern: the medieval Jewish commentators Radak and Ralbag explained Saul's spirit as melancholy, a sickness of black bile. Critical scholars (C) add that early Israel traced all things to God (Isaiah 45:7; Amos 3:6); compare 2 Samuel 24:1, where the LORD incites David, with 1 Chronicles 21:1, where it is Satan. Music brings relief (16:23), which many find psychologically true.
orig: רוּחַ רָעָה מֵאֵת יְהוָה (ruach ra'ah me'et YHWH)

a: the lyre
p: The kinnor was a small, hand-held stringed instrument, not a large harp.
b: The kinnor is the oldest instrument named in the Bible: Jubal was "the ancestor of everyone who plays the lyre and the pipe" (Genesis 4:21). Pictures from Egypt and Canaan show it as a wooden frame with two arms and a crossbar, strung with gut, played with the fingers or a plectrum. Josephus says it had ten strings (Antiquities 7.306). The KJV "harp" suggests the large instrument of later times; "lyre" is closer. Music was believed to affect the spirit: a minstrel's playing brought the word of the LORD to Elisha (2 Kings 3:15).

a: He's a strong fighter and a soldier
p: Here David is already a warrior. In chapter 17 he is a boy who has never worn armor.
b: The servant calls David a gibbor chayil, a "mighty man of strength," and a "man of war." In chapter 17 Saul says he is only a youth (17:33), and David cannot walk in armor (17:39). Harmonizing readers (H) say the servant is praising David's courage against lions and bears, or that "man of war" means fit for war. Critical scholars (C) see one of several signs that chapters 16 and 17 come from two different accounts of how David came to court (see 17:55). The list of praises ends with the key line of the whole story: "the LORD is with him" (18:12; 18:14; 18:28).

a: Saul came to love him deeply
p: Saul, Jonathan, Michal, Israel and Judah all "love" David. The narrator never says whom David loves.
b: The verb 'ahav, "to love," follows David through these chapters: Saul (here), Jonathan (18:1; 18:3; 20:17), all Israel and Judah (18:16), Michal (18:20; 18:28), even Saul's servants (18:22). Scholars such as J. A. Thompson note that "love" in ancient treaties meant political loyalty: vassals "love" their overlord. So the word describes both feeling and allegiance. The narrator never says that David loves anyone in return until his lament for Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:26). Readers have taken that silence as a sign of David's reserve, or of a calculating streak the story wants us to notice.

a: Saul could breathe again
p: The Hebrew plays on ruach (spirit, wind) and ravach (to have room to breathe).
b: Word for word: "Saul had relief (ravach), and it was good for him, and the evil spirit (ruach) turned away from him." The two words sound alike. The Spirit of the LORD left Saul (16:14), an evil spirit came, and David's music brings back revach, breathing room. The scene closes the chapter with David doing for the king what the king cannot do for himself, a pattern repeated when David fights Goliath. In 18:10 and 19:9 the music no longer helps.

a: between Socoh and Azekah at Ephes-dammim
p: The Valley of Elah runs from the hills of Judah toward Philistine Gath. Its places can still be found.
b: Socoh (Khirbet Abbad) and Azekah (Tel Azekah) stand on opposite sides of the Valley of Elah, a broad valley in the Shephelah, the low hills between Philistia and Judah (Joshua 15:35). The valley was a natural road from Gath into the heart of Judah. Between them, on a ridge above the valley, excavators since 2007 have uncovered Khirbet Qeiyafa, a fortified town with two gates, dated by its excavators to around 1000 BC. Yosef Garfinkel and Saar Ganor identify it with Shaaraim ("two gates," 17:52) and see it as a Judahite fort of David's time. Others question the date, the identification, or who built it.

a: a champion
p: The Hebrew for champion is "the man of the in-between," the fighter who steps into the space between two armies.
b: Ish habbenayim appears only in this chapter (here and 17:23). It describes single combat: one man from each side fights in the open ground, and the result decides the battle. The custom is best known from Greek epic, where Paris and Menelaus fight before Troy (Iliad 3) and Hector challenges the Greeks (Iliad 7). Since the Philistines came from the Aegean world, many scholars see the challenge as a Philistine custom. The Egyptian story of Sinuhe also describes a single combat with a strong man of Canaan. Something similar happens at the pool of Gibeon (2 Samuel 2:14–16).

a: named Goliath
p: 2 Samuel 21:19 says Elhanan of Bethlehem killed Goliath of Gath. How do the two accounts fit?
b: A list of David's warriors says: "Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite struck down Goliath the Gittite, whose spear shaft was like a weaver's beam" (2 Samuel 21:19). 1 Chronicles 20:5 says Elhanan son of Jair killed "Lahmi the brother of Goliath." Readers answer in several ways. (1) Chronicles preserves the right text, and 2 Samuel 21:19 is a copying error ("Lahmi" and "Bethlehemite" look alike in Hebrew). (2) Elhanan was another name for David (the Targum and Rashi). (3) There were two giants named Goliath. (4) Many critical scholars (Halpern, McCarter) think Elhanan's deed was later credited to David. Notice that in 1 Samuel 17 the name Goliath appears only twice (17:4; 17:23); everywhere else he is "the Philistine."

a: from Gath
p: Gath was the largest Philistine city in this period and the last refuge of the Anakim.
b: Joshua says some Anakim, the tall people Israel feared, survived only in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod (Joshua 11:22). 2 Samuel 21:15–22 lists four warriors "born to the Rapha in Gath." Gath is Tell es-Safi, a large site excavated since 1996 by Aren Maeir. In the layers of the 900s BC the team found a potsherd with two names written in early letters, 'lwt and wlt, which are similar in form to the name Goliath. It does not mention the Goliath of the Bible, but it shows that names of that type were in use at Gath. The Talmud makes Goliath a son of Orpah, Ruth's sister-in-law (Sotah 42b).

a: a coat of scales
p: Bronze scales sewn on leather, bronze helmet and shin guards: the gear of an Aegean-style warrior.
b: Scale armor, made of hundreds of small bronze plates sewn onto a garment, is known from Egypt, Mesopotamia and Nuzi. Five thousand shekels is about 125 pounds (57 kg), very heavy for armor, and a sign of the man's size. Bronze greaves (shin guards) were typical of Greek warriors in Homer. Some scholars, such as Israel Finkelstein, argue that the description fits a Greek hoplite of the 600s BC better than a fighter of 1000 BC, and so reflects the writer's own time. Others answer that Aegean armor of this kind is attested much earlier, in the Mycenaean world from which the Philistines came.

a: a bronze javelin
p: The kidon has been taken as a javelin, a curved sword, or (in the KJV) a small shield.
b: Kidon appears again in David's reply: "with a sword, a spear and a javelin" (17:45). In Joshua 8:18 it is held up as a signal, which suits a spear or a curved sword. The Dead Sea War Scroll uses the word for a kind of sword, so some scholars translate "scimitar," a curved sickle-sword known from Canaanite and Egyptian art. The KJV's "target" (a small round shield) followed older Jewish guesses. Slung "between his shoulders," it was carried on his back, ready to hand.

a: like the beam on a weavers' loom
t: A spear like a weaver's beam
p: The comparison may be about the spear's thickness, or about a loop and cord for throwing it.
b: The traditional reading is that the shaft was as thick as the heavy wooden beam of a loom. Yigael Yadin suggested another reading: a "weaver's beam" was a heddle rod, fitted with loops of cord, and the comparison meant Goliath's spear had a loop and thong wound around it, as Aegean javelins did, to make it spin in flight. Either way, it was a weapon Israelites did not have. The iron head of six hundred shekels weighed about fifteen pounds (7 kg). The same phrase describes the spear of the Goliath killed by Elhanan (2 Samuel 21:19). On the Hebrew written text ("arrow") and the scribes' reading ("shaft"), see the topic on Ketiv and Qere.

a: I am the Philistine
p: Goliath calls himself "the Philistine," and the narrator mostly does the same.
b: Goliath sets himself up as the Philistines in one man, just as he wants Israel to send one man to stand for Israel (17:9). The narrator follows his lead and names him only twice (17:4; 17:23), calling him "the Philistine" more than twenty-five times. Critical scholars who think the story was first told without his name take this as evidence (see the note on 17:4). Literary readers see another effect: the giant becomes less a person than the embodiment of the enemy, and David, on the other side, becomes Israel.

a: Today I throw my insults at the ranks of Israel
p: The verb charaf, "to taunt, insult," is the key word of the chapter.
b: Charaf means to scorn, taunt or disgrace, and the noun cherpah is "shame, disgrace." Goliath "insults" Israel's ranks (17:10; 17:25); David asks who can lift this "shame" off Israel (17:26) and says the Philistine has "insulted the battle lines of the living God" (17:26; 17:36; 17:45). For David the issue is not only Israel's honor but God's. The same verb describes the Assyrian Sennacherib, who sent messengers "to insult the living God" (2 Kings 19:4; Isaiah 37:4), and in both stories God answers the insult.

a: that Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judah
p: The Hebrew says "the son of this Ephrathite," as if the reader is meeting the family for the first time.
b: Chapter 16 already introduced Jesse, his sons and David. Here the narrator starts again: "David was the son of this Ephrathite ... whose name was Jesse," and names the three oldest sons a second time (17:13). The word "this" (hazzeh) may point back to 16:1–13 ("that Ephrathite we met"), as harmonizing readers say, or may be a sign that a second, independent story begins here, as Tov and others argue. Ephrathah was the clan or district of Bethlehem (Ruth 1:2; Micah 5:2). This verse begins the long passage missing from the oldest Greek text (17:12–31; see the textual note).

a: well on in years
p: The Hebrew says Jesse "came among men." The Plain follows the Syriac and some Greek manuscripts: "came into years."
b: The Masoretic Text reads ba ba'anashim, "he went among men," which makes little sense here. The Syriac and the Lucianic Greek read "advanced in years," which suggests a Hebrew bashanim, "in years," the usual idiom for old age (Genesis 24:1; Joshua 13:1). The change is one letter. The verse is also part of the long passage the Old Greek lacks (see the textual note).

a: David used to come and go between Saul's service and shepherding his father's flock
p: This verse explains why David, Saul's armor-bearer in chapter 16, is at home with the sheep in chapter 17.
b: Harmonizing readers (H) take the verse at its word: David served Saul part-time and went home when needed, perhaps because the king had others to carry his armor in war. Critical readers (C) see the verse as an editor's link, written to join two accounts: one in which David came to court as a musician (16:14–23), and one in which he was an unknown shepherd boy (17:12–31). The verse belongs to the section the Old Greek lacks, so in the shorter Greek text no bridge was needed. Literary readers note that the verse sets David between two worlds, court and pasture, as the story itself does.

a: forty days running
p: Forty is the Bible's number for a full time of testing.
b: The rain of the Flood fell forty days (Genesis 7:12), Moses was forty days on the mountain (Exodus 24:18), the spies searched the land forty days (Numbers 13:25), Israel wandered forty years, Elijah walked forty days to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8), and Jesus fasted forty days in the wilderness (Matthew 4:2). Here the number marks Israel's long humiliation: morning and evening, for a full period, no one answers the challenge. The detail also prepares for David's arrival, when the long test ends in a moment.

a: get some token from them
p: Jesse wants something from his sons to show they are alive, or perhaps their pay to bring home.
b: Arubbatam tiqqach means "take their pledge" or "their token." Most think Jesse wanted a sign that the brothers were well, such as a personal item or a message. Others suggest a pledge in the sense of a debt or payment, such as the brothers' wages or a guarantee for supplies. The Targum reads "bring back news of them." The detail shows a worried father with three sons at the front and no way to hear from them.

a: he will make his father's family free in Israel
p: Wealth, a royal bride, and freedom from royal duties: the reward shows what kings demanded of ordinary families.
b: Chofshi, "free," is the word for a slave set free (Exodus 21:2). Here it probably means free of the king's taxes and forced labor, the very burdens Samuel had warned about (8:11–17). The promise of the king's daughter will drive the plot of chapter 18, where Saul hands out his daughters as traps. The Talmud lists Saul's offer among three careless requests: the winner might have been a slave or of unfit birth, and still Saul had promised his daughter (Ta'anit 4a).

a: the living God
p: David sets the living God of Israel against a man who trusts in his size and his gods.
b: "The living God" (elohim chayyim) is the God who speaks and acts, unlike idols that cannot (Deuteronomy 5:26; Joshua 3:10; Jeremiah 10:10). Hezekiah uses the same words when Sennacherib's commander "insults the living God" (2 Kings 19:4), and the Psalms speak of thirsting for "the living God" (Psalm 42:2; Psalm 84:2). David's question turns a military crisis into a test of whose God is real, which is how the whole contest is framed in 17:45–47.

a: Eliab flared up in anger at David
p: Eliab, passed over at the anointing, mocks his youngest brother the way Joseph's brothers mocked him.
b: Eliab had stood before Samuel and been rejected (16:6–7); David was anointed "among his brothers" (16:13). Now Eliab accuses David of pride and a bad heart. Readers often compare Joseph, the younger son sent by his father to check on his brothers in the field, whom they hated (Genesis 37:12–20). The irony is sharp: the LORD had said he looks at the heart (16:7), and now Eliab claims to know David's heart. David's answer is short and he turns away (17:29–30).

a: It was just talk, wasn't it?
p: David's reply is two Hebrew words that can be read several ways.
b: Halo davar hu means "Is it not a word/a thing?" The KJV took it as "Is there not a cause?" (that is, "I have a reason to be here"). Most modern readers hear "It was only a question!" or "Can't I even speak?" Some take it as "Isn't this a matter worth asking about?" The Plain English chooses the plainest sense, an annoyed younger brother's reply: he was only talking.

a: A lion would come, or a bear
p: Lions and bears lived in Judah then. A shepherd had to defend the flock with his life.
b: Asiatic lions and Syrian brown bears survived in the land into the Middle Ages; the Bible mentions both often (Judges 14:5; 2 Kings 2:24; Amos 3:12; Amos 5:19). A shepherd was responsible for the animals in his care and had to show proof if a wild beast took one (Genesis 31:39; Exodus 22:13; Amos 3:12). David's speech is more than a boast: the ancient Near East commonly called kings "shepherds," and Israel's God would say of David, "You are the one who will shepherd my people Israel" (2 Samuel 5:2). Ezekiel 34 and John 10 build on the same image.
r: Judges 14:5–6; 2 Kings 2:24; Amos 3:12; Genesis 31:39; Exodus 22:13; 2 Samuel 5:2; Psalm 78:70–72; Ezekiel 34:23; John 10:11

a: and the LORD will be with you
p: Saul says it as a wish or a hope. The narrator says it as a fact about David.
b: The servant had said "the LORD is with him" (16:18). Saul now says it to David, perhaps as a blessing, perhaps without much thought. The narrator repeats it as the explanation of David's whole rise: "the LORD was with him" (18:12; 18:14; 18:28; 2 Samuel 5:10). Critical scholars (C) who read 1 Samuel 16 to 2 Samuel 5 as a defense of David's claim to the throne call this the theme of the "History of David's Rise." Traditional readers (H) hear the same line said of Joseph (Genesis 39:2–3) and Joshua (Joshua 6:27), and see David as the next in that line.

a: Saul put his own battle clothes on David
p: Saul, the tallest man in Israel, dresses the shepherd in his own armor. It does not fit.
b: Saul was a head taller than anyone (9:2; 10:23), the obvious man to fight Goliath, yet he stays in camp. When he puts his own clothing and helmet on David, the scene is full of meaning: the king's armor will not fit the new king, and David will not win by Saul's methods. Soon Jonathan will give David his own robe and weapons (18:4), this time freely, as a sign of covenant. And David will win wearing nothing but a shepherd's gear. Readers have long seen in this a picture of faith that does not rely on borrowed strength.

a: five smooth stones
p: A sling was not a toy. In skilled hands it was a deadly weapon with longer range than a spear.
b: A sling is a pouch with two cords. The slinger whirls it and lets one cord go, sending a stone the size of a tennis ball or larger at high speed. Benjaminite slingers could "hit a single hair with a slingstone, never missing" (Judges 20:16). Assyrian reliefs of the siege of Lachish show slingers in the front lines, and sling stones have been found at many sites. Against a heavily armored man with a spear and a shield-bearer, a sling let David strike from out of reach. Why five stones? The text does not say; later interpreters guessed at Goliath's four relatives (2 Samuel 21:22) or read the stones as symbols.

a: the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel's battle lines
p: David ties the title YHWH tseva'ot to "Israel's battle lines," showing one of its meanings.
b: On the title itself, see the note on 1:3. The armies may be the heavenly ones, angels or stars (1 Kings 22:19; Isaiah 40:26), or Israel's own (Exodus 7:4; Exodus 12:41). Here David chooses the second sense, or joins the two: the God of the heavenly armies is also "the God of Israel's battle lines," which Goliath has insulted (17:10; 17:26). The title was tied to the ark, the LORD's throne (4:4), which had once gone out with Israel's army and been lost. Now the LORD of Armies wins without ark or army.

a: Then all the earth will know there is a God who belongs to Israel
t: So that the whole earth will know
p: David's aim is the same one God announced at the Exodus: that all nations know who the true God is.
b: God hardened Pharaoh "so that my name will be told in all the earth" (Exodus 9:16). Joshua's crossing of the Jordan happened "so that all the peoples of the earth would know how strong the LORD's hand is" (Joshua 4:24). Elijah prays on Carmel, "today make it known that you are God in Israel" (1 Kings 18:36), and Hezekiah prays that "every kingdom on earth will know" (2 Kings 19:19). David puts his fight in this line. The audience is not only Israel and Philistia but "all the earth."

a: The battle belongs to the LORD
p: David's line is echoed by later prophets and became a motto of faith in war and in spiritual struggle.
b: Moses told Israel at the sea: "The LORD will fight for you" (Exodus 14:14). Jahaziel tells King Jehoshaphat and Judah, "The battle does not belong to you. It belongs to God" (2 Chronicles 20:15), and Zechariah and Hosea say God saves not by bow or sword (Zechariah 4:6; Hosea 1:7). Psalm 44:6–7 says the same. Judas Maccabeus told his outnumbered men, "Winning a war is not a matter of how big an army is. Strength comes from Heaven" (1 Maccabees 3:19). Christian readers have applied David's words to the believer's struggles, seeing Christ as the true David who fights for his people (Colossians 2:15). Jewish readers have read the story as a lesson in trust, and the rabbis praised David for giving the victory to God.
r: Exodus 14:14; 2 Chronicles 20:15; Psalm 44:6–7; Hosea 1:7; Zechariah 4:6; Colossians 2:15; 1 Maccabees 3:18–19

a: The stone sank deep into his forehead
t: Did the stone hit his forehead?
p: Goliath wore a bronze helmet. The Greek adds that the stone went "through the helmet."
b: The Septuagint reads that the stone sank "through the helmet into his forehead," perhaps to explain how it got past the bronze. Most readers think the helmet left the face and brow open, as many ancient helmets did. Ariella Deem suggested another reading: the Hebrew metsach, "forehead," is very close to mitschat, the word for his "shin guard" (17:6).
