If the stone struck the gap at his knee, the giant would fall forward "face down," as the verse says. Most commentators keep "forehead."

a: finished him off
p: 17:50 says David killed Goliath with the stone; 17:51 says he killed him with the sword.
b: Verse 50 says David "struck the Philistine and put him to death" with a sling and no sword; verse 51 says he took the giant's sword and killed him with it. Harmonizing readers say the stone stunned or mortally wounded Goliath, and the sword finished him. Critical scholars point out that 17:50 is one of the verses missing in the Old Greek and suggest it is a summary from the longer version, which makes the doublet. The point of 17:50 is theological: "David had no sword in his hand." The giant's own sword will later be kept at Nob and given to David (21:9).

a: David carried the Philistine's head to Jerusalem
p: Jerusalem was a Jebusite city until David captured it as king (2 Samuel 5:6–9).
b: Why would young David bring the head to a foreign city? Several explanations are offered. (1) The note looks ahead: later, as king, David brought the trophy to his capital. (2) The head was shown in the Israelite area outside the Jebusite fortress. (3) It is an editor's comment from a later time. "His own tent" is also puzzling, since David had just arrived from home; it may mean his family's tent or quarters later on. The sword itself turns up at the shrine of Nob, near Jerusalem (21:9). A later Jewish hero did the same: after Nicanor fell, Judas Maccabeus ordered his head cut off and taken to Jerusalem (2 Maccabees 15:30), in a book Catholic and Orthodox churches hold as Scripture, though Protestants and Jews do not.

a: Whose son is this lad, Abner?
t: Why does Saul not know David?
p: In chapter 16 David is Saul's beloved armor-bearer. Here Saul asks who he is. Readers explain this in several ways.
b: Harmonizing readers (H) give several answers. Saul is asking about David's father, not David, because he had promised freedom to the winner's family (17:25). Or Saul's illness had clouded his memory. Or chapter 16 is not in time order. Or David had grown and changed. Critical scholars (C) see two versions of how David met Saul, woven together. Emanuel Tov and Johan Lust argue that the Old Greek, which lacks 17:55–18:5, translates an earlier, shorter Hebrew story, to which a second story was added. Dominique Barthélemy and D. W. Gooding argue instead that the Greek translator, or the Hebrew text he used, cut passages to remove the problems. See the chapter page.

a: The son of your servant Jesse, the Bethlehemite
p: David's answer names his father, which is what Saul's reward depended on.
b: Saul's question was "whose son" (17:55; 17:56; 17:58), and David answers with his father's name and town. This supports the reading that Saul wanted to know the family he had promised to free (17:25). David's words also echo the servant's first description of him in 16:18 ("one of Jesse's sons, the Bethlehemite"). From now on Saul will call David "the son of Jesse," often with contempt (20:27; 20:30–31; 22:7–9).

a: Jonathan's life was tied up with David's life
p: The Hebrew says Jonathan's nefesh was "bound" to David's. The same words describe Jacob's love for Benjamin.
b: Nefesh is "life" or "self," and the verb qashar means to tie or bind. Judah says of Jacob and Benjamin, "his life is bound up with the boy's life" (Genesis 44:30), the love of a father for a son. Elsewhere qashar is used of conspiracy: people "binding" themselves together against a king (22:8; 22:13). Here the bond is devotion. The narrator says it begins the moment David finished speaking with Saul, at the high point of David's victory.
orig: וְנֶפֶשׁ יְהוֹנָתָן נִקְשְׁרָה בְּנֶפֶשׁ דָּוִד (wenefesh yehonatan niqsherah benefesh dawid)

a: Jonathan loved him
p: Jonathan's love for David has been read as covenant loyalty, as deep friendship, and by some as romantic love.
b: Readers give three main answers. (1) Covenant loyalty: ancient treaties use "love" for a vassal's loyalty (the Amarna letters; Deuteronomy 6:5), and J. A. Thompson reads Jonathan, the heir, binding himself to the future king; the robe and weapons (18:4) and his later words (23:17) hand over his claim. (2) Friendship: the traditional Jewish and Christian reading, the love "that does not depend on anything" (Mishnah Avot 5:16). (3) Romantic or erotic love: Tom Horner and Susan Ackerman point to Jonathan's "delight" in David (19:1, a verb used of Shechem's desire for Dinah, Genesis 34:19), Saul's taunt about "nakedness" (20:30), and 2 Samuel 1:26. Most commentators read covenant friendship; a substantial minority sees homoerotic overtones. See the chapter page.

a: Jonathan stripped off the robe he had on and gave it to David
p: Jonathan gives the heir's robe and weapons to David. Without a word, he hands over his place.
b: Clothing marks status in Samuel: Samuel's robe was torn as a sign of the kingdom torn from Saul (15:27–28), and David will cut a corner of Saul's robe (24:4). Saul's armor did not fit David (17:38–39); Jonathan's gift is freely given. Exchanging garments and weapons sealed friendships among warriors in the ancient world (compare Glaucus and Diomedes in Iliad 6). Many readers see Jonathan as quietly giving David his right to the throne, which he will say openly later (23:17).

a: Saul has struck his thousands
p: The song uses a common pattern of Hebrew poetry. Saul hears an insult in it.
b: Hebrew poetry often pairs a number with a larger one in the second line ("thousand ... ten thousand": Deuteronomy 32:30; Psalm 91:7; Micah 6:7). The women may have meant only to praise both men. But Saul hears the comparison and draws the conclusion: "The only thing still missing for him is the kingship!" (18:8). The song became famous; even the Philistines quote it (21:11; 29:5). Women greeting returning warriors with song and tambourine recalls Miriam (Exodus 15:20) and Jephthah's daughter (Judges 11:34).

a: he fell into a prophet's frenzy
p: The same verb that describes inspired prophets here describes Saul's raving.
b: Yitnabbe is the reflexive form of "prophesy," used of the ecstatic prophets Saul met in 10:5–13 and of the prophets of Baal on Carmel, who "raved" (1 Kings 18:29). Here, under an evil spirit, it means frenzied behavior. Many English versions say "raved." The Plain English keeps the link to prophecy, because the narrator uses one word for Saul's high point (10:10) and his low points (18:10; 19:23–24).

a: an evil spirit from God swept down on Saul
p: The spirit that troubled Saul in 16:14 comes back, and this time Saul turns violent.
b: On the meaning of "evil spirit from God," see the note on 16:14 and the topic. The verb is tsalach, "swept down," the same verb used when the Spirit of the LORD came on Saul for good (10:6; 11:6) and on David (16:13). The writer uses it here on purpose: the force that once empowered Saul now torments him. Josephus speaks of demons; Radak and Ralbag of melancholy; Christian interpreters have often spoken of a judgment that hands a hardened man over to what he has chosen. This verse and the next are missing from the Old Greek (see the textual note).

a: Saul threw the spear
p: Saul's spear is always near him. It becomes a sign of his rule and of his danger.
b: Saul sits with a spear in hand (19:9; 22:6), throws it at David twice (18:11; 19:10) and at his own son (20:33). David will later take Saul's spear from beside his head as he sleeps and refuse to use it (26:7–12). On Gilboa, Saul leans on his spear as he dies (2 Samuel 1:6). Some ancient readers took the spear as a royal symbol, like a scepter. The repeated image shows a king who no longer rules by God's favor, only by force.

a: from Saul he had turned away
p: The verb echoes 16:14 and looks ahead to 28:15, where Saul himself will say it.
b: The LORD's Spirit "turned away from Saul" in 16:14; here the narrator repeats it. At En-dor Saul will use the same verb when he tells the ghost of Samuel that God "has gone away from me" (28:15), and Samuel will answer that the LORD has turned away from him (28:16). Saul's fear of David is in the end a fear of the God who is with David and not with him. The Old Greek has only "Saul was afraid of David"; these words are absent there (see the textual note).

a: David was loved by all Israel and Judah
p: Even here the writer names Israel and Judah separately, as if looking ahead to two kingdoms.
b: In 1 Samuel the army is counted as Israel and Judah separately (11:8; 15:4; 17:52). After Saul's death Judah will make David king at Hebron while Israel follows Saul's son (2 Samuel 2:4–10), and after Solomon the two will split for good (1 Kings 12). Some scholars see the pairing as the writer's later perspective; others see it as evidence that the tribes were already loosely joined under Saul. The verse also explains how David could later become king of both: he was popular in both.

a: fight the LORD's wars
p: Saul speaks of holy war while planning David's death. The narrator lets us hear his inner thoughts.
b: The "Wars of the LORD" was a name for Israel's battles (Numbers 21:14 mentions a book by that name), and later Abigail will say David "fights the LORD's wars" (25:28). In Saul's mouth the phrase is a cover. The narrator lets us overhear him: "Let it be the Philistines' hand on him." Readers often compare David's own later plan to have Uriah killed by the Ammonites (2 Samuel 11:14–17), where David repeats Saul's sin.

a: Adriel the Meholathite
p: Merab marries Adriel. Her five sons will later die in a grim story in 2 Samuel 21.
b: In 2 Samuel 21:8 most Hebrew manuscripts say the five sons of "Michal" whom she bore to Adriel were handed to the Gibeonites. Since Michal married Paltiel, not Adriel (25:44), most translations follow two Hebrew manuscripts and the Greek and read "Merab." The Talmud keeps "Michal" and says she raised her sister's children (Sanhedrin 19b). Abel-meholah was the town in the Jordan valley that later was Elisha's home (1 Kings 19:16).

a: Michal, Saul's daughter, loved David
p: Michal is the only woman in the Bible's stories said to love a man. David's feelings are never stated.
b: Robert Alter and others note that many people are said to love David: Jonathan (18:1), all Israel and Judah (18:16), Michal (18:20; 18:28), even Saul at first (16:21). But the text never says David loved any of them. Literary readers (L) take this as part of David's mystery: he is loved, and he wins, and we rarely see his heart. J. Cheryl Exum traces Michal's tragedy from love here to contempt in 2 Samuel 6:16. Traditional readers (H, J) see a loving wife who saves her husband's life (19:11–17).

a: a hundred Philistine foreskins
p: Saul's demand is a cruel joke: the uncircumcised enemy will pay David's bride-price, or kill him.
b: A bride-price (mohar) was paid by the groom to the bride's family (Genesis 34:12; Exodus 22:16–17). Saul says he wants none, only proof that David has killed a hundred Philistines. Taking a part of the body as a battle count is known from Egypt: reliefs of Ramesses III at Medinet Habu show scribes counting heaps of hands and phalluses cut from dead Libyan enemies, who, like the Philistines, were uncircumcised. The Philistines were Israel's uncircumcised enemy (14:6; 17:26). David brings twice the number (18:27, Hebrew).

a: His name came to be greatly valued
p: The chapter ends with David's name prized. God will later promise him "a great name."
b: Wayyiqar shemo me'od: "his name became very precious." The LORD will say to David through Nathan, "I will give you a name as great as the names of the great men on the earth" (2 Samuel 7:9), as he promised Abraham (Genesis 12:2). The rise is complete: the shepherd is now the most famous man in Saul's army. But this verse is one of those missing from the Old Greek (see the textual note).

a: took great delight in David
p: Chafets, "to delight," is the same word Saul's servants used when luring David into marriage.
b: Saul had told his servants to say, "The king is delighted with you" (18:22), a lie. Jonathan's delight is real. The same verb is used when the LORD "delights" in someone (2 Samuel 15:26; 2 Samuel 22:20; 1 Kings 10:9) and when Samuel asked whether the LORD "delights" in offerings as much as in obedience (15:22). Jonathan now has to choose between his father and his friend.

a: why would you sin against innocent blood
p: Jonathan uses the language of the law: shedding innocent blood brings guilt on the land.
b: Deuteronomy warns against shedding "innocent blood" and the guilt it brings on the land (Deuteronomy 19:10; Deuteronomy 21:8–9; Deuteronomy 27:25). Later prophets say the same of kings who killed innocent people (2 Kings 21:16; 2 Kings 24:4; Jeremiah 22:17). Jonathan speaks to his father as the king who ought to uphold the law. Abigail will later keep David himself from shedding blood without cause (25:26; 25:31).

a: he shall not be killed
p: Saul swears by the LORD that David will not die, and soon tries to kill him again.
b: Saul's oaths go wrong throughout his story. His rash oath almost killed Jonathan (14:24; 14:39; 14:44); here his oath to spare David lasts only a few verses (19:9–10). He will swear again to the medium at En-dor (28:10). Some readers (H) think Saul meant it and was overcome by the evil spirit. Others (L) see a man who means what he says only for the moment. Jonathan, by contrast, keeps every oath he makes (20:16–17; 20:42).

a: an evil spirit from the LORD came over Saul
p: The scene of 18:10–11 happens again almost word for word.
b: Some readers (H) take this as a second attack, showing Saul's illness getting worse. Critical scholars (C) note that 18:10–11 is missing from the Old Greek, and suggest that the scene in 18:10–11 was copied from here, or that two versions of one event were kept. Literary readers (L) note the repetition sharpens the drama: Saul had just sworn by the LORD (19:6), and the spear flies anyway.

a: Michal lowered David through the window
p: Rahab lowered the spies from her window; Paul was lowered from a window in Damascus.
b: Rahab let the spies down "by a rope through the window" (Joshua 2:15), and Paul was lowered from a window in the wall of Damascus in a basket (Acts 9:25; 2 Corinthians 11:33). Each time a woman or friends save God's messenger from a king's men by the same trick. Psalm 59's heading links that psalm to this night, "when Saul sent men to watch the house in order to kill him." Many think the heading was added later, but it shows how early readers connected David's prayers with his life.

a: the household god
p: Teraphim were household images. Why David's house had one has puzzled readers.
b: Teraphim are household gods or images, perhaps of ancestors, used in divination (Ezekiel 21:21; Zechariah 10:2). Rachel stole Laban's (Genesis 31:19) and hid them by sitting on them, also fooling her father. Samuel had just named teraphim together with rebellion (15:23). This one was large enough to pass for a man in bed. Some readers (H) suggest it was Michal's, not David's. The Targum and some rabbis avoid the problem by saying it was a dummy, not a god. Others see the detail as honest about popular religion in Israel.

a: a mat of goat hair
p: The rare word kevir may mean a net, a quilt, or a mat of goat hair that looked like a man's hair.
b: Kevir ha'izzim appears only here and in 19:16. Some take it as a net or a fly-net over the face, others as a pillow stuffed with goat hair, others as a woven piece of black goat hair that looked like a man's hair on the pillow. The Greek read "a goat's liver," perhaps from a similar Hebrew word, and Josephus says Michal put a beating goat's liver in the bed to make it look like a breathing man (Antiquities 6.217). The exact meaning is uncertain.

a: Let me go, or must I kill you?
p: Michal lies to protect David and herself. Readers judge her lie in different ways.
b: Like Rahab (Joshua 2:4–6) and the Hebrew midwives (Exodus 1:19), Michal deceives a ruler to save a life. Her lie to Saul also protects her from his anger. Augustine, who held that every lie is sin, counted such lies as less guilty but still wrong. Many later Christian and Jewish readers have argued that deceiving a murderer is permitted or even right. The narrator does not comment, though the story clearly sides with Michal against Saul's plan.

a: Naioth
p: The name may mean "dwellings" or "camps," perhaps the quarters of the prophets at Ramah.
b: Nayot appears only in this story. It is probably not a separate town but a place within or near Ramah, since the text always says "Naioth in Ramah." The word may come from naweh, "pasture, dwelling," and refer to the huts where the company of prophets lived. The Targum translates it "house of study" (bet ulpana), and Jewish tradition pictured Samuel's school of prophets there.

a: the company of prophets prophesying
p: Groups of ecstatic prophets, here led by Samuel, are known in Israel and in its neighbors.
b: Saul met a group of prophets with music in 10:5. Later, groups called "sons of the prophets" gather around Elijah and Elisha (2 Kings 2:3; 2 Kings 4:38). In the wider ancient world, letters from Mari on the Euphrates (1700s BC) describe ecstatic prophets, and an Egyptian tale (Wenamun, around 1100 BC) tells of a young man falling into a frenzy in Byblos. Here Samuel stands over the group, as its leader. The word for "company" (lahaqah) appears only here; the Greek and Syriac read "assembly."

a: they began prophesying as well
p: Three times Saul sends men, and three times the Spirit stops them. Then Saul goes himself.
b: The pattern recalls 2 Kings 1:9–15, where King Ahaziah sends three captains with fifty men to seize Elijah. Here no one is harmed; the Spirit simply overwhelms them. Numbers 11:25–29 tells of the Spirit falling on seventy elders and on two men in the camp, and Moses wishing all the LORD's people were prophets. Here the Spirit protects God's anointed against the king who has lost the Spirit.

a: lay naked all that day and all that night
p: Saul strips off his clothes and falls down before Samuel. It is a picture of humiliation.
b: "Naked" (arom) can mean fully naked or stripped down to an undergarment (Isaiah 20:2–4; John 21:7). Saul, whose robe was torn (15:27) and whose armor did not fit David, now loses even his clothes. He lies helpless before the prophet who anointed and rejected him. Some readers see God's protection of David; others see compassion, a last touch of the Spirit on the rejected king. This was the last time Saul saw Samuel alive (15:35); they meet once more at En-dor (28:11–19).

a: Is Saul also among the prophets?
p: The saying is explained in 10:11–12 and again here. Is it praise or a joke?
b: In 10:11–12 the saying arises when Saul joins the prophets after his anointing, a sign of the Spirit on him. Here it arises in disgrace. Harmonizing readers (H) say the proverb arose in chapter 10 and was repeated here with a bitter twist. Critical scholars (C) see two stories explaining one popular saying. Either way, the saying was probably a mockery of someone acting out of character, like "Is Saul a prophet now?" Robert Alter notes that the second story reverses the first: the Spirit that made Saul king now undoes him.

a: I am one step away from death
p: David's vivid phrase became a common saying for mortal danger.
b: Literally, "there is but a step between me and death." David has dodged the spear twice (18:11; 19:10) and escaped through a window (19:12). Jonathan still cannot believe his father means it (20:2). The phrase sets up the test of the new moon: Jonathan will learn the truth only when the spear is thrown at him (20:33).

a: Tomorrow is the new moon
p: The first day of each month was a holy day with sacrifices and a meal, as the Law commanded.
b: Israel's months began with the new moon. The Law commands burnt offerings "at the beginnings of your months" and trumpet blasts "on the first day of each month" (Numbers 28:11–15; Numbers 10:10). Prophets mention new moons with Sabbaths as days when trade stopped and people visited prophets (2 Kings 4:23; Amos 8:5; Isaiah 1:13–14). Saul's table on the new moon was a royal feast, and attendance was expected. Saul assumes David missed it because he was ritually unclean (20:26), since those eating sacrificial meat had to be clean (Leviticus 7:20–21).
r: 20:26; Numbers 10:10; Numbers 28:11–15; 2 Kings 4:23; Amos 8:5; Isaiah 1:13–14; Leviticus 7:20–21

a: the yearly sacrifice there for the whole clan
p: Clans held their own yearly sacrifice in their home towns, as Elkanah's family did at Shiloh.
b: Elkanah went up "year after year" to sacrifice at Shiloh (1:3; 1:21), and Samuel held a sacrifice at Bethlehem with Jesse's family (16:2–5). A clan (mishpachah) was a group of related households. Before Jerusalem's temple became the only place of sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12; 2 Kings 23), such local feasts were common. David's excuse is believable, but it is a lie, and Jonathan repeats it to his father (20:28–29).

a: Deal with your servant in loyal love
p: Hesed is the loyal love owed within a covenant. David appeals to the covenant Jonathan made.
b: Chesed is kindness that goes beyond duty, loyalty within a bond. David reminds Jonathan of their covenant (18:3), calling it "a covenant of the LORD" because the LORD was witness to it. Jonathan answers by asking for the same loyal love for himself and his family when David comes to power (20:14–15). Years later David will ask, "Is there anyone left of Saul's house, so that I may show him loyal love for Jonathan's sake?" and will take in Jonathan's son Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9:1–7).

a: the LORD do so to Jonathan and more besides
p: This is a common oath form: the speaker calls down a curse on himself if he fails.
b: The full form was probably spoken with a gesture, as if to say "May the LORD do this to me (cut me like an animal) and worse." Eli used it with Samuel (3:17), Saul with Jonathan (14:44), Ruth with Naomi (Ruth 1:17). The phrase links to the ancient way of making a covenant by cutting animals in two and walking between them (Genesis 15:9–17; Jeremiah 34:18–20). Here Jonathan curses himself if he does not warn his friend.

a: The LORD be with you, the way he was with my father
p: Jonathan blesses David as Saul's successor. He knows who the next king will be.
b: "The LORD be with you" is what the narrator keeps saying of David (16:18; 18:12; 18:14). Jonathan prays it as the LORD was once with Saul, a prayer that only makes sense if David will take Saul's place. In 20:15 he speaks of the LORD cutting off David's enemies, and in 23:17 he says plainly, "You are the one who will reign over Israel, and I will be next to you." Readers (H, J) see a model of humility; others (C) see the hand of a writer defending David's claim to the throne, in which even Saul's heir gives David his blessing.

a: So Jonathan cut a covenant with David's house
p: Hebrew says covenants are "cut," and this verse plays on the word.
b: Karat berit, "cut a covenant," is the regular Hebrew phrase, probably from the cutting of animals in covenant ceremonies (Genesis 15:10; Jeremiah 34:18). In 20:15 Jonathan asks David never to "cut off" his loyal love, even when the LORD "cuts off" David's enemies. Then he "cuts" a covenant. The Plain English keeps "cut" in all three places to show the play. The second half of the verse is awkward in Hebrew; it may be a polite way of saying "may the LORD punish David if he breaks it."
orig: וַיִּכְרֹת יְהוֹנָתָן עִם־בֵּית דָּוִד (wayyikhrot yehonatan 'im-beit dawid)

a: He loved him with the love he had for his own life
p: The phrase echoes 18:1 and 18:3, and the command to love one's neighbor as oneself.
b: Literally "for the love of his soul he loved him." Some readers hear an echo of Leviticus 19:18, "love your neighbor as yourself." Jewish tradition holds up this friendship as the model of love "not dependent on anything" (Mishnah Avot 5:16), unlike Amnon's love for Tamar, which died when he got what he wanted (2 Samuel 13:15). David's lament for Jonathan says, "Your love was a wonder to me, / more than the love of women" (2 Samuel 1:26). On the debate about the nature of their love, see the note on 18:1 and the topic.

a: Tomorrow is the new moon
p: When the new moon falls on a Sunday, synagogues read this chapter.
b: In Jewish practice, when the Sabbath falls on the day before a new moon (Rosh Chodesh), the prophetic reading (haftarah) after the Torah is 1 Samuel 20:18–42, called Machar Chodesh from its opening words, "Tomorrow is the new moon." The custom is mentioned in the Talmud (Megillah 31a). The reading gives a picture of loyalty in hard times, and a prayer for the coming month.

a: the spot where you hid on the day of that business before
p: The Hebrew is obscure: "the day of the deed" may point back to 19:2–3, when David hid in a field.
b: Beyom hamma'aseh means "on the day of the deed/the business." It probably refers to the earlier time Jonathan told David to hide while he spoke to Saul (19:2–3). Others think it means "on the working day," that is, the day after the feast. The Greek reads differently. The stone "Ezel" is also uncertain; see the textual note.

a: He's not clean
p: Saul guesses David is ritually unclean and so cannot eat the sacred meal.
b: A person who had touched a dead body, had a bodily discharge, or the like was "unclean" until evening or longer (Leviticus 15:16; Leviticus 22:4–7; Numbers 19:11). Eating sacrificial meat while unclean was forbidden (Leviticus 7:20–21). The new moon meal was sacred, so an unclean guest stayed home for a day. But by the second day, Saul's patience runs out.

a: the son of Jesse
p: Saul refuses to say David's name. He calls him only "the son of Jesse."
b: To call a man only by his father's name, especially a humble one, could be an insult, like saying "that nobody." Saul will do it again and again (20:30–31; 22:7–9; 22:13), and Doeg and Nabal will copy it (22:9; 25:10). The rebel Sheba will use it too: "We have no share in David, no inheritance in the son of Jesse!" (2 Samuel 20:1). In the Psalms and Isaiah, though, "the son of Jesse" and "the stump of Jesse" become names of honor (Psalm 72:20; Isaiah 11:1).

a: You son of a twisted woman, a rebel!
p: Saul's insult attacks Jonathan through his mother. It is the kind of curse that turns shame back on the speaker.
b: Literally "son of a perverse woman of rebellion." The Greek reads "son of runaway girls." Saul adds "the nakedness of your mother," that is, the shame of the womb that bore him; since Jonathan's mother is Saul's own wife Ahinoam (14:50), the insult falls back on Saul. Readers who see a homoerotic bond (Horner, Ackerman) note that 'ervah, "nakedness," is the regular word in the sexual laws (Leviticus 18) and hear in "you have picked the son of Jesse" a sexual accusation. Most commentators (Alter, McCarter) hear political betrayal: Saul goes on to say Jonathan's kingship is at stake (20:31), and "nakedness of your mother" is a curse on his birth.

a: He is a son of death!
p: A Hebrew idiom: someone who deserves death, or is marked to die.
b: "Son of" in Hebrew can describe what a person belongs to or deserves: a "son of strength" is a brave man, a "son of wickedness" a wicked one. "Son of death" means "he must die." David will use the same phrase twice: of the rich man in Nathan's parable (2 Samuel 12:5), and of Saul's guards who failed to protect the king (26:16). Ironically, David pronounces his own sentence in 2 Samuel 12:5 and is told "You are the man."

a: Saul threw the spear at him
t: The spear at his own son
p: The spear meant for David is now thrown at Jonathan. Saul's rage has no limits.
b: Saul had been ready to kill Jonathan once before, for breaking an oath he did not know about (14:44). Now Saul throws the spear at his son. Jonathan finally knows that his father intends to kill David (20:33), and he leaves the table in anger and grief. Some readers compare Saul with the jealous king Herod, who killed his own sons; others with Jacob's sons who hated Joseph. Jonathan's loyalty to both father and friend will last until he dies beside Saul on Gilboa (31:2).

a: bowed three times
p: David bows three times to Jonathan, the king's son, as a sign of respect and humility.
b: Bowing to the ground was the respect given to a superior (Genesis 33:3, seven times; 2 Samuel 9:6). David still treats Jonathan as the prince, though Jonathan has already treated him as the future king. Then the two kiss and weep, as relatives and close friends did at partings (Genesis 33:4; Genesis 45:14–15; Ruth 1:9). "Until David's weeping grew greatest" is a hard phrase; the Greek reads "until a great end," and some take it to mean David wept the most, or "until David controlled himself."

a: between my offspring and your offspring, for all time
p: Jonathan's covenant reaches to his descendants. David will keep it with Mephibosheth.
b: Jonathan made the covenant with "David's house" (20:16), not with David alone. When David is king he will seek "anyone left of Saul's house" for Jonathan's sake and give Mephibosheth a place at his table (2 Samuel 9:1–13). When the Gibeonites demand seven of Saul's descendants, David spares Mephibosheth "because of the oath of the LORD between them, between David and Jonathan" (2 Samuel 21:7). This is one of the few promises in Samuel that is kept fully.
